clue.text: Shut up, therefore

indicators.note: When something is up it is amiss, out of its proper order, and letters that are up come out of theirs too.

parts.note: four letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A curt order to be quiet, with a reason tacked on as though it followed from an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shut up' is the raw material, not the meaning, and the one word after the comma is all the answer has to match. Four-letter anagrams hide best when the fodder sits in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: therefore → THUS: both introduce the consequence that follows from what has just been said, THUS being the more formal of the two.

clue.text: Evidence of foul play from tabloids? No kidding!

indicators.note: To be kidding is to be messing about instead of playing it straight, and letters messed about with land in a new order.

parts.note: eight letters of fodder
the two letters that bring the fodder up to ten

explanation.surface: Mock astonishment at the news that the red-tops have been caught out in something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No kidding!' reads as one exclamation of disbelief, which is exactly what hides the split the setter needs: half of it is material and half of it is instruction. The question mark marks the seam.
explanation.definitionFit: Evidence of foul play → BLOODSTAIN: the mark blood leaves on a carpet or a cuff, and the first thing an investigator reads as a sign of violence.

clue.text: Thingummyjig had holes, 500, all around

indicators.note: Turning a thing all the way around leaves it facing the other way, so the letters gathered before it are read back to front.

parts.note: the word itself, taken whole
two holes drawn as two rings
the Roman numeral for five hundred, with the whole run then read backwards

explanation.surface: A gadget remembered only for the holes all over it and a price of five hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thingummyjig' announces that the answer is one of the joke words English keeps for objects whose name has escaped you. Nothing points at the direction of travel except the clue's last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Thingummyjig → DOODAH: both are placeholder words for a contraption whose real name you cannot bring to mind.

clue.text: Lots killed

definitions.meaning: a great number of something, as in a whole heap of them
the past tense of slay, the verb of dragons and giants

explanation.surface: A body count from some battle, delivered in two flat words.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase the two words are one grim report, and that reading is the trap: each has to stand alone. The noun came into English from Irish and the verb from Old English, which is why they share a spelling by accident.
explanation.definitionFit: Lots → SLEW: a slew of letters or visitors is a great many of them; killed → SLEW: the past tense of slay, what the dragon-killer did.

clue.text: I may bum around just like that time, getting muscle weakness

indicators.note: To bum around is to drift with no fixed route or order, which is what the letters beside it do.

parts.note: four letters of fodder
'just like this' and 'as this' say the same thing
the time being pointed at is then

explanation.surface: Someone admitting they drifted about back in those days exactly as everyone else did.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder arrives as three innocent scraps — a pronoun, a comparison, a time — so there is no solid-looking word to shuffle and nothing to count until you try. Only the medical definition at the end is straight.
explanation.definitionFit: muscle weakness → MYASTHENIA: the medical name for muscles that tire and fail under use, best known from myasthenia gravis.

clue.text: Model youngster eating in

indicators.note: What is eaten goes inside the eater, so the short word after it is swallowed by the letters before.

parts.note: a pup is a young animal, opened up to take the insert
the word itself, dropped whole into the middle

explanation.surface: A small boy wolfing his tea down indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture of a child at the table keeps 'in' looking like part of the meal rather than a word to be swallowed letter for letter. 'Model' is the fashion sense, and the enumeration warns that the answer comes in two chunks.
explanation.definitionFit: Model → PIN-UP: the glamour photograph pinned to a wall, and by extension the person who poses for one.

clue.text: Ratify in advance President Trump's first meeting with a politician

parts.note: the everyday short form, as on a nameplate

indicators.note: Two things that meet are set side by side, so the pieces are simply written one after another.

parts.note: the letter the name starts with
the article taken as it stands
a Member of Parliament, the crossword's standard politician

explanation.surface: A newly sworn-in president holding his first meeting with a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Rubber-stamping is where the definition lives: to stamp a thing is to put approval on it, and the prefix moves that approval ahead of the event. The surface offers a diary entry instead of an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratify in advance → PRESTAMP: to stamp is to mark with approval, and the PRE- puts that approval in place before the thing it approves happens.

clue.text: One moving between banks, somewhat penniless

indicators.note: Somewhat means only part of the thing, so only part of the word beside it is wanted — a run of its letters, in order.

parts.note: letters four to seven running straight on: penNILEss

explanation.surface: A broke traveller going from one bank to the next with nothing to put in either.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' are the money sort on the surface and the muddy sort in the definition, which is the whole misdirection. Only one word in the clue is long enough to bury four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: One moving between banks → NILE: a river runs between two banks, and this is the longest of them, so the definition names one by example.

clue.text: Indestructibility of a neck hair on neck regularly ignored, note

parts.note: 'twice a day' and 'twice per day' say the same thing
the long hair along a horse's neck

indicators.note: Regular letters are the ones at even steps through a word, and ignoring them leaves the rest standing in order.

parts.note: the first and third letters of the word, the second and fourth thrown away
a note of the scale, which runs A to G

explanation.surface: A memo about how long a single hair from a horse's neck survives when nobody notices it.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'neck' is used twice over, once for the hair that grows there and once as four letters to be thinned out, and the two jobs sit side by side. A note as E is a convention worth owning early.
explanation.definitionFit: Indestructibility → PERMANENCE: what cannot be destroyed goes on lasting, and permanence is the noun for that lasting quality.

clue.text: That man will start to organise welcome

parts.note: he'll is the contraction of 'he will', that man being he

indicators.note: the start of the next word means only its opening letter is used

parts.note: its first letter supplies the final piece

explanation.surface: A man promising to get a welcome party organised.
explanation.walkthrough: HE'LL, with its apostrophe dropped as crosswords do, is 'That man will'; 'start to' takes just the O of organise.
explanation.definitionFit: Hello is the word of greeting used to welcome someone.

clue.text: Film legal professional losing weight

indicators.note: What is lost has gone from what held it, so the letter named next drops out of the word before.

parts.note: the solicitor or barrister, with one letter then taken out
w is the standard short form for weight

explanation.surface: A barrister on a diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' is the thin-coating sense — a film of dust, a film of oil — and not the cinema the word wants to suggest. The letter that goes is named by its abbreviation rather than described.
explanation.definitionFit: Film → LAYER: a film of dust or grease is one thin layer of it spread over a surface.

clue.text: Declines important information Nazi group has pinched

indicators.note: To pinch a thing is to grip it between two points, so the letters named close on the word sitting between them.

parts.note: Hitler's paramilitary corps, its two letters split to sit either side
the lowdown is the inside story on something

explanation.surface: A refusal to accept intelligence that the SS has stolen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Declines' is a plural noun here, the dips a graph makes, not the verb the sentence offers. 'Pinched' looks like theft and is asking for a grip.
explanation.definitionFit: Declines → SLOWDOWNS: when trade or output loses pace, each such fall is a slowdown, the word the business pages use for a decline.

clue.text: Dodgy mate's in hot water

indicators.note: A dodgy thing cannot be trusted to be what it says, and dodgy letters will not stay in the order they are given.

parts.note: five letters to rearrange, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: An unreliable friend who has landed himself in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In hot water' is the idiom the surface sells, meaning in trouble, and the definition is only the last two words of it, meant literally. The apostrophe counts for nothing in an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: hot water → STEAM: water heated past boiling becomes steam, so the phrase names it by what it is made of.

clue.text: Fruit with it revolted at first

indicators.note: What comes at first comes at the front, so the piece it follows leads and the other falls in behind.

parts.note: a people who revolted rose against their rulers
with-it and hip both mean up to the minute

explanation.surface: Some fruit that was fashionable and rebelled early on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' is a position and not a time, which is the one thing the clue asks you to re-read. A rose's fruit is the swollen red hip left standing when the petals have gone, picked for syrup and tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit → ROSEHIP: the red-orange fruit a rose carries once it has finished flowering.

clue.text: American right-winger concerning landlord

parts.note: re = concerning, as at the head of a memo
the publican is the licensee who keeps a pub

explanation.surface: A conservative American with something to say about his landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: A landlord in Britain is most often the licensee who keeps a pub, the name painted above its door, rather than whoever owns your flat. The two pieces run in clue order, so the only work is finding the join.
explanation.definitionFit: American right-winger → REPUBLICAN: a member of the more conservative of the two big US parties, named by example of the political right.

clue.text: Bit of excess gas, sir, turned up after favourite part of massage

indicators.note: the reversed piece comes after the favourite, so it follows it in the answer

parts.note: a pet is a favourite, as in teacher's pet

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means the letters are read from bottom to top
a bit of the word means just its first letter

parts.note: its opening letter begins the reversed run
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An embarrassing burp of gas during a massage, with an apology to sir.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'Bit of excess' as a separate end piece; it joins the run 'turned up', so EGASSIR becomes RISSAGE. Petrissage is a French-derived massage term.
explanation.definitionFit: Petrissage is the kneading technique in massage, one of its standard strokes.

clue.text: Boost and pick up most of football team

indicators.note: Most of a thing is nearly all of it and never quite all, so the number wanted is one short of the full side.

parts.note: to pick up a sound or a signal is to hear it
a football side is eleven players, and most of eleven is ten

explanation.surface: A manager told to lift the side and collect nearly all of its players.
explanation.walkthrough: The arithmetic is the trick: eleven take the field, so most of them is one fewer, and the answer needs a number rather than a word for the squad. 'Pick up' is the hearing sense, as in picking up a signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Boost → HEARTEN: to hearten people is to put heart into them, the lift to morale that boosting a team means.

clue.text: Scruffy beard hater is agitated

indicators.note: Agitating something shakes its contents out of place, and shaken letters settle in a new order.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A clean-shaven man worked up about other people's facial hair.
explanation.walkthrough: Ten letters of fodder sit in plain sight as a phrase that means something on its own, which is an anagram's best disguise. The definition is the first word, where it reads as description.
explanation.definitionFit: Scruffy → THREADBARE: cloth worn until its threads show through looks shabby, so a threadbare coat is a scruffy one.

clue.text: Approval in place before statement of account

indicators.note: What comes before a thing is written in front of it, so the short piece leads.

parts.note: Pl. is the short form on street signs and envelopes
an audit is the formal going-over of the books that states how the accounts stand

explanation.surface: A nod of approval given on the spot, just before the accounts are read out.
explanation.walkthrough: The short form for place is the one on street signs — Portland Pl. — and it arrives with no signal beyond the word itself. Everything after 'before' belongs to the world of bookkeeping, which is where the surface wants you to stay.
explanation.definitionFit: Approval → PLAUDIT: a plaudit is a burst of praise or applause, approval said out loud.

clue.text: After reflecting, made statement covering speculation on representative's ultimate condition

indicators.note: A reflection hands a thing back to you the other way round, so the word that follows is read in reverse.
A cover goes over what lies beneath it, so the letters named next are taken inside.
In a down answer one thing on another sits above it, so the first of these two pieces is written first.

parts.note: whoever made a statement said something, and the four letters are then turned round
a bet is money staked on a guess
the last letter of the word representative

explanation.surface: A considered statement addressing rumours about how a delegate's health finally stood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Representative's ultimate' is the last letter of the word itself, not of anybody in the story, and that is the step most solvers miss. The definition is the single word at the end, doing duty as medical shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: condition → DIABETES: a long-term disorder of blood sugar, the kind of illness described as a condition because you live with it rather than recover from it.

clue.text: Introduction from Nora Ephron that takes the piss

indicators.note: the introduction of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: its first letter starts the answer
the surname is used as written

explanation.surface: An introduction to the writer Nora Ephron that mocks its subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Introduction from' Nora gives N. Nora Ephron was an American screenwriter (When Harry Met Sally). 'Takes the piss' looks like mockery, but read literally it is what a kidney filter does.
explanation.definitionFit: A nephron is the tiny filtering unit of the kidney, which draws urine out of the blood.

clue.text: Language derived from English in Indonesian island

indicators.note: In puts one thing inside another, so the letters before it go within the word named after.

parts.note: Bali, the Hindu island east of Java, opened up to take the insert
Eng. is the standard short form for English

explanation.surface: A creole that grew out of English spoken on an Indonesian island.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface promises a pidgin and the answer is nothing of the kind — it is the tongue of Bangladesh, with no English in it beyond three borrowed letters. 'Derived from' does nothing but join the halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Language → BENGALI: the tongue of Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal, spoken by well over two hundred million people.

clue.text: Union losing millions in old feudal system

definitions.note: Arriage is a service owed under the old Scottish feudal system rather than a name for the system itself; the setter names the system to place a word most solvers will never have met.

indicators.note: What is lost has gone, so the letter named next is dropped from the word before it.

parts.note: a marriage is the union of two people, with one letter then taken away
m is the standard short form for millions

explanation.surface: A trade union haemorrhaging millions of pounds under an old arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' is the marriage sense, not the trade sort the surface offers, and that swap is the whole of the wordplay. Arriage belongs to old Scots law: the horse-work a tenant owed his lord, always named alongside carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: old feudal system → ARRIAGE: under Scottish feudal tenure this was the servitude of horse-labour a tenant owed the landlord, the pair 'arriage and carriage' naming his dues.

clue.text: Thin official entering shaft

indicators.note: Whoever enters a room ends up inside it, so the letters before the word sit within the ones after.

parts.note: a shaft of light is a ray of it, opened up to take the insert
the referee who officiates a match

explanation.surface: A skinny official climbing down a mine shaft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thin' is a verb here, which is why no adjective will fit. The shaft is the one light comes in, not the one sunk into the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin → RAREFY: to rarefy is to make less dense, as air does with altitude, so it matches 'thin' used as a verb.

clue.text: Type of music in decline

parts.note: the word itself, taken whole
a wind or a fire that declines dies away

explanation.surface: A genre of music that is steadily losing its audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Independent labels rather than the majors gave the genre its name and its guitars. 'Decline' is the fading sense, not the refusing one the grammar of the sentence invites.
explanation.definitionFit: Type of music → INDIE: guitar music put out by independent labels, a recognised genre in its own right since the 1980s.

clue.text: Blue drink

definitions.meaning: low in spirits, the mood the blues are named for
the verb for swallowing a pint straight off, in one go

explanation.surface: A cocktail the colour of the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two separate meanings, and the trap is reading them as one phrase about a coloured drink. Neither half is doing anything to the other's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue → DOWN: feeling down is feeling low in spirits, the same flatness blue names; drink → DOWN: to down something is to swallow it straight off.

clue.text: In building for horses, always open to influence

indicators.note: In places one thing within another, so the word for always is set inside the word for the building.

parts.note: the stable is where horses are housed, opened up to take the insert
e'er is the poet's clipped form of ever

explanation.surface: A stabled horse that will always do as it is told.
explanation.walkthrough: E'er for always is a contraction the crossword keeps alive long after the poets stopped using it. The comma is placed so that 'always' looks like part of the description rather than material.
explanation.definitionFit: open to influence → STEERABLE: anything steerable can be pushed one way or another by whoever has hold of it, which is what being influenced amounts to.

clue.text: Obtain Listener solution at last

parts.note: the ear is the organ that does the listening

indicators.note: What comes at last is the final one, so only the closing letter of the word before is taken.

parts.note: the last letter of the word solution

explanation.surface: Finally getting hold of the answer to a Listener puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics point at the Listener crossword, the hardest weekly puzzle in Britain, so the clue reads as relief rather than as an instruction. 'At last' is the setter's standard way of asking for a final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Obtain → EARN: to earn a thing is to come by it through deserving it, the getting that follows having worked for it.

clue.text: Garden weed endangered hosts

indicators.note: A host has guests staying inside the house, so the words before it are keeping something within them.

parts.note: the letters run straight on across the gap: weED ENdangered

explanation.surface: A weed in the flowerbed threatening the plants it has taken hold of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garden' alone is the definition and it slips past as one more piece of horticulture. Hidden words that straddle two words of the clue are the hardest kind to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Garden → EDEN: the garden of Genesis, familiar enough that 'the Garden' on its own names it.

clue.text: Composer left in furious state after review

indicators.note: In puts one thing inside another, so the letter named is set within the word beside it.
To review is to look back over, and a word looked back over is read from its end to its start.

parts.note: a furious state is a rage, and these four letters are then read backwards
l is the standard short form for left

explanation.surface: A songwriter abandoned in a temper once the critics have had their say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Review' is the looking-back sense and not the critic's notice the surface is selling, which is the one word to re-read. Elgar wrote the Enigma Variations and Land of Hope and Glory.
explanation.definitionFit: Composer → ELGAR: Edward Elgar, of the Enigma Variations and the Pomp and Circumstance marches, named here by example.

clue.text: Loud warning about Tesla

indicators.note: Something placed about a thing is wrapped round it, so the word before closes on the letter after.

parts.note: fore is the shout a golfer gives to warn whoever is ahead, opened up to take the insert
T is the symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density

explanation.surface: Somebody shouting a warning about an electric car.
explanation.walkthrough: Tesla is the car maker on the surface and the unit of magnetism in the wordplay, both named after the same Serbian engineer. 'Loud' is the direction printed in a score rather than a description of the shout.
explanation.definitionFit: Loud → FORTE: the marking in a score telling a player to play loudly, Italian for strong.

clue.text: New jokes for 5th of November?

definitions.note: The answer looks plural but names a single day, and the date is given as one example because that day falls on the fifth in most months and the seventh in the rest.

parts.note: n is the standard short form for new
'have you heard the one about...' — a one is a joke

explanation.surface: Fresh gags being written for Bonfire Night.
explanation.walkthrough: The fifth of November is Bonfire Night in Britain, and that is the decoy. The Roman calendar had its own name for that date, falling on the fifth of most months and the seventh of March, May, July and October.
explanation.definitionFit: 5th of November? → NONES: in the Roman calendar the nones fell on the fifth of November, so the date names the day.
